summary:
This bill is called the Kids Internet and Digital Safety Act, or the KIDS Act. Its main job is to create new rules to protect people under 17 when they are online.

The bill sets up age checks for websites that mostly show sexual material harmful to kids. These sites must use a special tool to figure out if a user is a minor and block them from seeing that content. They cannot keep the personal data used for the age check any longer than necessary. This part starts one year after the bill becomes law.

For social media platforms, the bill requires safety settings. Platforms must offer tools so kids and parents can limit who can message them, stop features that make the app hard to stop using, and control sharing of their location. The default setting must be the most private and safe choice. Platforms must also give parents a way to see and change their child's privacy settings and screen time. Platforms have to hire an outside auditor every year to check how they are doing and make a public report within 45 days of finishing.

The bill bans disappearing messages for all minors. It bans direct messaging for kids under 13. For teens 13 and older, platforms must give parents controls to approve contacts and manage who can message them. It stops platforms from studying minors like test subjects for market research, unless it is to make the platform safer. These changes take effect between 90 and 180 days after the bill becomes law.

For online video games that connect to the internet, the bill says the game provider must give parents tools to limit who their child talks to, restrict purchases, and set time limits. These safety controls must be turned on and set to the most protective level by default.

The bill also makes rules for AI chatbots. A chatbot must tell a minor that it is not a real person and suggest a break if a chat has lasted for three hours. It must also provide a suicide prevention hotline number if asked about suicide. A chatbot cannot lie and say it is a doctor or other licensed professional.

The law asks for several government studies. These include a study on how social media affects kids' mental health, a report on whether minors can buy dangerous drugs like fentanyl through social media, and a four-year study on how chatbots affect kids' loneliness and anxiety. It also creates a public education campaign to teach online safety and a special partnership to share best practices.

The general rules of the bill start one year after it is passed. The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general can enforce the law.
